extracted.intended_audience: historians and textual critics researching d'Argenson, editors of 18th-century French texts, and archival scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and criteria for judging the authenticity, provenance, and dating of a disputed memoir or edition, illustrated from the case of d'Argenson; includes internal-textual, archival, and editorial-signature evidence. Useful for editors, bibliographers, and historians establishing whether a document is genuine and when/revisions it was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: presence among ordinary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Probable unauthenticity if a memoir 'has not been discovered by [other scholars] among the ordinary sources' and is nowhere referred to in the author's published memoirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence from commonly known source-collections is a prima-facie ground for suspicion, but not definitive: absence must be weighed against other evidence (manuscript copies, internal likeness to known texts, references elsewhere). The author rebuts the argument from absence by showing independent signs of authenticity (see other criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance inferred from internal cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement 'certainly unimportant' was based on the claim that the memoir is 'nowhere referred to, as it assuredly would have been, in d'Argenson's Memoirs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars may infer a document's importance if it is cited within an author's corpus; conversely, lack of citation is used to argue unimportance — but this inference depends on whether the relevant portion of the corpus was actually edited/published. If portions are unedited or lost, absence of citation is not decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual similarity and transcriptional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large portions of Flassan's text are 'positively little else than a verbal transcription from d'Argenson' with wholesale appropriation and only occasional word changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim correspondence, repeated passages, and parallel phrasing between the suspect memoir and authenticated manuscripts indicate common source or authorship. Look for identical phrasing, transposition of paragraphs, and instances where small word changes were made — these patterns support authenticity or direct dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript provenance and use of author's original manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flassan's account derives from 'the original manuscripts then in possession of the d'Argenson family, and afterwards in the Library of the Louvre,' and his transcription was executed before later printed editions existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance (possession history) of manuscripts and evidence that an editor worked from the author's originals strongly support authenticity. Establish chain-of-custody (family papers, library holdings, dates of transcription) and whether the editor had access to the relevant manuscripts at the claimed time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on contemporaneous letters and papers as corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Flassan lacked edited memoirs for a period, he relied on 'letters and papers of Marshal de Noailles' and other original materials as additional sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent documentary corroboration (letters, official papers, third-party journals) that align with the disputed memoir strengthens claims of authenticity. Cross-check events, dates, and factual claims with other archival documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial insertion patterns and composition clues
rubrics_metrics.description: The memoir's appearance is 'peculiar': it is inserted with brief introductions, wedged amidst verbatim extracts from other texts, and followed by sections taken word for word from d'Argenson — a pattern suggesting reliance on his manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the memoir is embedded in the editor's volume: abrupt insertions, juxtaposition with known texts, and the presence of editor-introductions can indicate the editor was reproducing manuscript material rather than inventing it. Patterns of transposition and abrupt transitions are diagnostic of editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction or loss of originals as an explanatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Memoir and d'Argenson's manuscripts 'perished in the burning of the Library of the Louvre in 1871,' which explains non-appearance in later searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When originals are known to have been destroyed or lost, absence in later catalogs or failure of later scholars to find a text is not strong evidence against authenticity. Accounting for losses in archival history is essential before rejecting a text on negative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dating editions by internal textual comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1764 and 1784 texts were dated by collating differences: additions/omissions of chapters, changes in expressions, appearance/disappearance of a 'plan,' topical references (e.g., 'The House of Nassau') and shifts in tone — internal clues pointing to composition or revision dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic collations between editions to identify revised passages, new chapters, altered phrasing, and topical references. Minor shifts of expression, changes in references to contemporary persons/events, and the inclusion or removal of thematic plan-statements can date revisions (in this case suggesting a revision c.1748-1752 and a later revision c.1755). Examples from the text (e.g., phrase substitutions and added chapters) illustrate how specific lines anchor dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of distinct 'plans' or intellectual phases within an edition
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1784 edition divides into two parts representing different plans: (a) chapters I–VI and VIII are a revised portion of the original work; (b) chapters VII, IX, and Conclusion represent a later, markedly different plan and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and separate distinct intellectual projects or 'plans' present within a single edition by noting thematic discontinuities, abrupt changes in purpose, and chapters directed to different schemes. These divisions suggest multiple revision phases and can be dated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of slight verbal touches as chronological markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle shifts in wording (e.g., 'les vertus sociales' for 'des manières polies') and other small phrase-changes serve as evidence of revision and relative dating between editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog and compare minor lexical or idiomatic differences across versions; these 'slight touches' often accumulate into convincing internal evidence for a revision timeline, especially when combined with larger structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing of themes for locating author's positions in journals/memoirs
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendices present detailed indexes ('D'ARGENSON'S VIEWS ON PUBLIC QUESTIONS' and 'INDEX TO THE GREAT PUBLIC QUESTIONS'), mapping topics to volume/page references in the journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating or consulting thorough topical indexes of an author's journals and memoirs assists in locating where key public questions are treated, which aids both authentication and assessment of importance. Use compiled references to verify whether an idea or memoir would reasonably be expected to be mentioned elsewhere in the corpus.
